$comment: Golden fixtures for the Lunora wire value codec (shared/wire-codec.ts).
`cases[].encoded` is the canonical JSON wire form. A conforming codec MUST
satisfy `encode(decode(encoded)) == encoded`, which exercises both the decode
of tagged tokens and their re-encode.
A few shapes are legitimately NOT fixed points of that identity — a bare
`[TAG]` array is escaped on the way back out; an object field that arrives
as the `undefined` tag is dropped, matching JSON.stringify; a `bytes` tag
naming an unknown typed-array ctor decodes to raw bytes and re-encodes
without the name; and a `map` carrying a duplicate key collapses last-wins,
because the reference decodes into a real Map; and a `date` epoch is put
through TimeClip on the way in (truncated toward zero, and replaced by an
Invalid Date past ±8.64e15 or when non-finite), so it re-encodes as the
clipped value rather than the one on the wire. Those carry `reencoded`, and
the assertion becomes `encode(decode(encoded)) == reencoded`. Without it
those shapes were untestable, so no port was held to them — four decoded
the first two differently, all eight kept the unknown ctor name and both
duplicate entries, and all eight round-tripped an out-of-range epoch back
onto the wire as a date no reference decoder will accept.
`proto-key` and `error-proto-key` are the same assertion in the two places a
wire object is rebuilt — a bare object and an `error` tag's props slot. They
are a JS-only hazard (`__proto__` is an ordinary map key in the other seven
languages, which is why all eight ports passed them before the reference did),
and they only pin round-trip fidelity here: an assignment fires the prototype
SETTER, so the field never becomes an own property and re-encodes as `{}`.
`rejected[]` is the other half: wire values every port MUST refuse to decode.
It is data for the same reason the case list is — a rejection each suite
hard-codes for itself is a rejection only some suites have.
The base64 entries pin CANONICITY, not merely decodability: a `bytes` payload
must be exactly the string the encoder would have written for those bytes.
`atob` and most standard-library decoders are far more forgiving than that —
they strip embedded whitespace, infer missing padding, and discard the unused
low bits of a short final quantum — and the eight ports inherited whichever
subset of that leniency their language happened to ship, landing 3-accept /
5-reject on an unpadded payload alone. Worse, the lenient reading of `"AQJ="`
is not a divergence but a silent rewrite: it decodes to the two bytes 01 02
and re-encodes as `"AQI="`, different bytes than the peer wrote. So the six
base64 rejections here cover every shape of that: 1 mod 4 (truncated), 3 mod 4
(unpadded), padding in the middle, a newline, an interior space, a non-zero
trailing bit under one `=` and under two, the base64url alphabet, and a
non-ASCII character (which python's decoder rejects with a BARE ValueError
rather than its own binascii.Error, so the codec's rejection was not the
codec's type — the same contract break Java's Map.entry NPE was).
The rest of `rejected[]` is what a hand-rolled decoder waves through where
the reference throws: a map entry that is not EXACTLY a pair (reading slots
0 and 1 out of a longer one is the same invention as inventing a missing
half); a `set`/`arr` payload that is not an array (a string iterates per
CHARACTER); a typed-array payload that is not a whole number of elements
(`new Float32Array` on 3 bytes raises a RangeError); an `error` tag whose
props slot is not an object — missing or null (`Object.keys` throws on
both), or a string/number/boolean/array, where `Object.keys` does NOT
throw but enumerates a primitive wrapper, so `[TAG,"error","E","m","ab"]`
would decode with the invented props `{0:"a",1:"b"}`; and a bigint
tag with a missing or non-ASCII digit string (`\d` is ASCII-only, while a
Unicode-aware digit test accepts Arabic-Indic ٣).
A tag's payload slot is TYPE-CHECKED, never coerced: a `date` epoch that is
not a number (`null` coerces to epoch 0, a string to an Invalid Date, and a
boolean to epoch 0 or 1 — the last of which a language whose number type
bridges booleans, such as Swift's NSNumber, accepts unless it checks), a
`bytes` payload that is not a string (`atob(null)` decodes the base64 of
"null" — three invented bytes), and a `url` href that is not a string (a
one-element array ToStrings into a parseable href). Each of those decoded,
and re-encoded as a plausible value, which is what makes them worse than a
throw; every port already refused them.
The `error` name and message slots are type-checked the same way, and were
the last two that were not. Six ports substituted `""` for a non-string in
either slot — erasing the error's identity while accepting the frame — two
carried the non-string through verbatim, and the reference ToString-coerced
the message while passing the name through, so one malformed frame produced
three different errors across nine implementations. A slot that must hold a
string and does not is a malformed frame, like every other slot here.
A `url` href must additionally be ABSOLUTE — a scheme, then the rest. The
reference builds a real `URL`, which throws on anything else, while all eight
ports stored the string verbatim and accepted `"not a url"`: a frame that kills
a JS peer's subscription and is waved through everywhere else. Ports are not
asked to reproduce WHATWG URL parsing (they cannot, and their language parsers
disagree with it in the deep end); the scheme check is the floor, and these
three entries are what it must catch.
Language-native construction checks (e.g. bigint 7 -> the bigint tag, or an
integer past the exact-float64 range being refused) live in each SDK's own
suite, keyed by protocol/conformance-cases.json, since native values are not
uniformly JSON-representable.

cases.$comment: TimeClip runs ToIntegerOrInfinity, which returns +0 for every epoch in (-1, 0] — truncation alone keeps the sign of zero and yields -0. The window is one value wide either side of zero, which is why `date-epoch-fractional-negative` (-1.5 -> -1) misses it, and it is not cosmetic: `stable-key` spells -0 as the bare token `-0`, distinct from `0`, so a port that truncates opens a different subscription than the TS client for the same Date. Written `-0.5` and `-0.0` rather than `-0`, so a JSON parser that narrows an integral literal to an integer cannot drop the sign before the codec sees it.
cases.name: date-epoch-negative-fraction

cases.$comment: SameValueZero holds -0 equal to 0, so a signed zero collapses onto an unsigned one in both a set and a map. Spelled `-0.0` rather than `-0` on purpose: a JSON parser that reads an integral literal as an integer drops the sign before the codec sees it, which would make this pass vacuously.
cases.name: set-duplicate-zero-signs

cases.$comment: `new Map([["k", null]])` is an ordinary return value and JSON carries null in both slots, so neither half of an entry may be routed through a pair type that refuses nulls. A port that does throws on every frame carrying one, and the throw is not even its own format error.
cases.name: map-null-value
